note: Life in the UK test course: 400 original practice questions written from the official handbook 'Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents' (3rd edition), tagged by chapter. Not the questions of the real test. Facts that changed after the handbook was printed (monarch, EU, devolved assembly sizes, amounts of money) are avoided. Teacher review recommended before publishing.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The fundamental principles of British life include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the fundamental principles of British life?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The fundamental principles are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life. Voting is not compulsory.

items.prompt: Which TWO are fundamental principles of British life?
distractors: Individual liberty and a state newspaper
Military service and a state newspaper
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Democracy and individual liberty are two of the fundamental principles of British life.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is one of the fundamental principles of British life.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of British life.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: British values and principles are based only on written laws, not on history or traditions.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The fundamental principles of British life are based on history and traditions and are protected by law, customs and expectations.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, the fundamental principles of British life are based on:
distractors: the wishes of the monarch alone
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): British values are based on history and traditions and are protected by law, customs and expectations.

items.prompt: If you wish to be a permanent resident or citizen of the UK, which of these should you do?
distractors: Buy a house in the UK
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Anyone who wishes to be a permanent resident or citizen should respect and obey the law.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: People who want to live permanently in the UK should look after the area in which they live and the environment.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Looking after the area in which you live and the environment is one of the responsibilities listed for permanent residents and citizens.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Respecting the rights of others includes respecting their right to their own opinions.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Permanent residents and citizens should respect the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions.

items.prompt: Which of these is a freedom that the UK offers to everyone living here?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): In return for the responsibilities, the UK offers freedoms including freedom of belief and religion and freedom of speech.

items.prompt: Which right does the UK offer to everyone living here?
items.answer: The right to a fair trial
distractors: The right to choose which laws to obey
The right to a company car
The right to free private healthcare
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The freedoms the UK offers include the right to a fair trial.

items.prompt: Which TWO are freedoms that the UK offers to people living here?
items.answer: Freedom of speech and the right to a fair trial
distractors: Freedom of speech and free housing
Free housing and a guaranteed job
The right to a fair trial and a guaranteed job
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The UK offers freedoms including freedom of speech, freedom of belief and religion, freedom from unfair discrimination, the right to a fair trial and the right to join in the election of a government.

items.prompt: Which of these is a responsibility of people who want to live permanently in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Permanent residents and citizens should treat others with fairness.

items.prompt: Among the responsibilities listed in the handbook, people should look after:
distractors: only people of their own faith
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): People who wish to be permanent residents or citizens should look after themselves and their family.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The right to join in the election of a government is one of the freedoms people in the UK enjoy.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The freedoms offered by the UK include the right to join in the election of a government.

items.prompt: At a citizenship ceremony, new citizens make an oath or affirmation of allegiance and a:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Applicants take part in a citizenship ceremony, where they make an oath (or affirmation) and a pledge.

items.prompt: In the oath or affirmation of allegiance, new citizens promise to be faithful to:
items.answer: the monarch, their heirs and successors
distractors: the Prime Minister of the day
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): In the oath or affirmation, new citizens promise to be faithful and bear true allegiance to the monarch, their heirs and successors, according to law.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to uphold the UK's democratic values.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The pledge includes: 'I will uphold its democratic values.'

items.prompt: Which of these promises is part of the citizenship pledge?
items.answer: To observe the UK's laws faithfully
distractors: To serve in the armed forces
To vote in every general election
To live in the UK for the rest of their life
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The pledge includes: 'I will observe its laws faithfully and fulfil my duties and obligations as a British citizen.'

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A person who does not wish to swear an oath by God can make an affirmation instead.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): At the citizenship ceremony applicants make either an oath (sworn by God) or an affirmation, which has no religious wording.

items.prompt: To become a permanent resident or a British citizen, you normally need to:
items.answer: speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK
distractors: own a property and have a UK driving licence
join a UK political party and vote in an election
have been born in a Commonwealth country
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): To apply to become a permanent resident or citizen you need to be able to speak and read English and have a good understanding of life in the UK.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The questions in the Life in the UK test are based on the official handbook.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The test questions are based on all parts of the handbook 'Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents'.

items.prompt: Where can you take the Life in the UK test?
items.answer: At a registered and approved test centre
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): You can only take the test at a registered and approved Life in the UK test centre.

items.prompt: The Life in the UK test is usually taken by people who are applying for:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Passing the Life in the UK test is part of the requirements for people applying for settlement (permanent residence) or British citizenship.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Only British citizens, and not other people living in the UK, are expected to respect and obey the law.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The responsibilities and freedoms that flow from the fundamental principles are shared by all those living in the UK.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT listed in the handbook as a responsibility of people who want to live permanently in the UK?
items.answer: Attending a religious service every week
distractors: Looking after the area where they live
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The listed responsibilities include respecting and obeying the law, respecting the rights of others, treating others with fairness, looking after yourself and your family, and looking after your area and the environment. Religion is a free choice.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Individual liberty means people in the UK may break the law if they disagree with it.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The rule of law is a fundamental principle of British life: everyone must respect and obey the law, whatever their personal views.

items.prompt: Which fundamental principle of British life is about the adult population having a say in how the country is governed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Democracy is one of the fundamental principles of British life: the adult population chooses its government.

items.prompt: Which TWO are responsibilities of people who want to live permanently in the UK?
items.answer: Obeying the law and treating others fairly
distractors: Obeying the law and voting in every election
Owning a home and treating others fairly
Owning a home and voting in every election
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Permanent residents and citizens should respect and obey the law and treat others with fairness.

items.prompt: Which countries make up the United Kingdom?
items.answer: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
distractors: England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: Which countries make up Great Britain?
distractors: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Great Britain refers only to England, Scotland and Wales.

items.prompt: What is the official name of the country?
items.answer: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
distractors: The United Kingdom of England and Ireland
The Kingdom of Great Britain and the Isles
The British Union of England and Scotland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The official name of the country is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are part of the United Kingdom.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are not part of the UK; they are Crown dependencies with their own governments.

items.prompt: What are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man known as?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies, closely linked with the UK but not part of it.

items.prompt: Which TWO are British overseas territories?
items.answer: St Helena and the Falkland Islands
distractors: St Helena and the Isle of Man
Jersey and the Isle of Man
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): There are several British overseas territories linked to the UK, such as St Helena and the Falkland Islands. Jersey and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Crown dependencies have their own governments.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man have their own governments and are called Crown dependencies.

items.prompt: Which cross on the Union Flag represents Scotland?
items.answer: A white diagonal cross on a blue ground
distractors: A red cross on a white ground
A red diagonal cross on a white ground
A yellow cross on a black ground
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The cross of St Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, is a white diagonal cross on a blue ground.

items.prompt: Which patron saint's cross on the Union Flag represents Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The cross of St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland, is a red diagonal cross on a white ground.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Wales is represented on the Union Flag.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick. Wales is not represented on it.

items.prompt: Why is the Welsh dragon not on the Union Flag?
items.answer: Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created
distractors: Wales chose not to be included in the design
The dragon was thought too difficult to show
Wales joined the United Kingdom after 1801
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The Welsh dragon does not appear because, when the first Union Flag was created, Wales was already united with England.

items.prompt: What is the national flag of the UK often called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The flag of the UK is the Union Flag, often called the Union Jack.

items.prompt: Which TWO cities are capitals of countries in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The capital cities are London (England), Edinburgh (Scotland), Cardiff (Wales) and Belfast (Northern Ireland).

items.prompt: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Belfast is the capital city of Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Glasgow is the capital city of Scotland.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Edinburgh is the capital city of Scotland.

items.prompt: What is the currency of the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The currency in the UK is the pound sterling; there are 100 pence in a pound.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Banknotes issued in Scotland and Northern Ireland are valid everywhere in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Northern Ireland and Scotland have their own banknotes, which are valid everywhere in the UK, although shops and businesses do not have to accept them.

items.prompt: Where is Gaelic, a different language from English, spoken?
items.answer: In some parts of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland
distractors: In Cardiff and the Welsh valleys
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): In Scotland, Gaelic is spoken in some parts of the Highlands and Islands.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In Northern Ireland, a number of people speak Irish Gaelic.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): A number of people in Northern Ireland speak Irish Gaelic.

items.prompt: Which TWO languages, other than English, are spoken in parts of the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Many people in Wales speak Welsh, which is taught in schools and universities, and Gaelic is spoken in parts of Scotland (Irish Gaelic in Northern Ireland).

items.prompt: When is St David's Day?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): St David is the patron saint of Wales; his day is 1 March.

items.prompt: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland.

items.prompt: On which date is St George's Day, the day of England's patron saint?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): St George's Day, England, is 23 April.

items.prompt: St Patrick's Day, 17 March, is the patron saint's day of which part of the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland; his day is 17 March.

items.prompt: Which TWO parts of the UK have their patron saint's day as an official holiday?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Only Scotland and Northern Ireland have their patron saint's day as an official holiday (although in Scotland not all businesses close).

items.prompt: Christmas Day, 25 December, celebrates:
distractors: the rising of Jesus from the dead
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Christmas Day celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ and is a public holiday.

items.prompt: When is Boxing Day?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Boxing Day is the day after Christmas Day, 26 December, and is a public holiday.

items.prompt: What is Shrove Tuesday also known as?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Shrove Tuesday, the day before Lent starts, is known as Pancake Day.

items.prompt: How long is Lent, the period before Easter?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Lent is the 40 days before Easter.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Easter marks the death of Jesus Christ on Good Friday and his rising from the dead on Easter Sunday.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Easter takes place in March or April and marks the death of Jesus on Good Friday and his rising from the dead on Easter Sunday.

items.prompt: What is Hogmanay?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay; 2 January is also a public holiday there.

items.prompt: Diwali is celebrated by:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Diwali is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs; it is often called the Festival of Lights.

items.prompt: Which city is famous for its Diwali celebrations?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): There is a famous Diwali celebration held in Leicester.

items.prompt: Which festival lasts eight days and remembers the Jewish people's struggle for religious freedom?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Hannukah is in November or December and is celebrated for eight days; a candle is lit on a stand (a menorah) each day.

items.prompt: Eid al-Fitr celebrates:
distractors: the victory of good over evil
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Eid al-Fitr celebrates the end of Ramadan, when Muslims have fasted for a month.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Eid ul Adha remembers that the prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son when God ordered him to.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Eid ul Adha remembers that the prophet Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son when God ordered him to.

items.prompt: Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival that celebrates:
items.answer: the founding of the Sikh community known as the Khalsa
distractors: the end of the month of Ramadan
the victory of good over evil
the beginning of the new year in Scotland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Vaisakhi (also spelled Baisakhi) is a Sikh festival celebrating the founding of the Sikh community known as the Khalsa.

items.prompt: On which day do people play jokes on each other until midday?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): April Fool's Day, 1 April, is a day when people play jokes on each other until midday.

items.prompt: When is Mothering Sunday?
items.answer: The Sunday three weeks before Easter
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) is the Sunday three weeks before Easter.

items.prompt: Bonfire Night, 5 November, remembers:
items.answer: a failed plan in 1605 to blow up the Houses of Parliament
distractors: the end of the First World War in 1918
the coronation of King James I in 1603
the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): In 1605 a group of Catholics led by Guy Fawkes failed in their plan to kill the Protestant king with a bomb in the Houses of Parliament.

items.prompt: Halloween, on 31 October, has its roots in an ancient pagan festival that marked:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Halloween is an ancient festival with roots in the pagan festival to mark the beginning of winter.

items.prompt: Remembrance Day, 11 November, commemorates:
items.answer: those who died fighting for the UK and its allies
distractors: the opening of the first Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Remembrance Day commemorates those who died fighting for the UK and its allies. It originally commemorated the dead of the First World War, which ended on 11 November 1918.

items.prompt: What do many people wear in the period before Remembrance Day?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): People wear poppies (the red flower found on the battlefields of the First World War).

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: On Remembrance Day there is a two-minute silence at 12 noon.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): At 11.00 am on 11 November there is a two-minute silence.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Bank holidays have a special religious meaning.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Bank holidays are public holidays of no religious significance, held at the beginning of May, in late May or early June, and in August.

items.prompt: Which TWO are Christian festivals?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Christmas and Easter are Christian festivals; Diwali is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs, and Vaisakhi by Sikhs.

items.prompt: Who is the head (Supreme Governor) of the Church of England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The monarch is the head of the Church of England.

items.prompt: Who is the spiritual leader of the Church of England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The spiritual leader of the Church of England is the Archbishop of Canterbury.

items.prompt: What kind of church is the Church of Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): In Scotland the national church is the Church of Scotland, which is a Presbyterian church.

items.prompt: Who chairs the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland and is appointed for one year only?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The chairperson of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland is the Moderator, who is appointed for one year only.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: There is an established (state) church in Wales.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): There is no established church in Wales or Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Everyone in the UK has the legal right to choose their religion, or to choose not to practise a religion.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Everyone has the legal right to choose their religion, or to choose not to practise a religion.

items.prompt: What is 'Big Ben'?
items.answer: The nickname of the great bell of the clock at the Houses of Parliament
distractors: The official name of the clock tower at Westminster
A famous bridge across the River Thames
The largest bell in St Paul's Cathedral
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Big Ben is the nickname for the great bell of the clock at the Houses of Parliament in London.

items.prompt: In 2012, the tower of the clock at the Houses of Parliament was named:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The tower was named Elizabeth Tower in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee in 2012.

items.prompt: Where is the Eden Project?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Eden Project is located in Cornwall, in the south west of England.

items.prompt: Which castle is a dominant feature of the skyline of Scotland's capital city?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Edinburgh Castle is a dominant feature of the skyline in Edinburgh, Scotland.

items.prompt: Where is the Giant's Causeway?
items.answer: On the north-east coast of Northern Ireland
distractors: On the west coast of Wales
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Giant's Causeway is located on the north-east coast of Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: Which was the first national park in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park was the first national park in Scotland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Loch Ness is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Loch Lomond is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.

items.prompt: The London Eye was originally built as part of the UK's celebration of:
distractors: the end of the Second World War
the opening of the Channel Tunnel
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The London Eye was originally built as part of the UK's celebration of the new millennium.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The London Eye stands on the northern bank of the River Thames.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The London Eye is situated on the southern bank of the River Thames.

items.prompt: Where is the Millennium Stadium, the national stadium of Wales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Millennium Stadium in Cardiff is the national stadium of Wales.

items.prompt: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Snowdonia is a national park in North Wales; its best-known landmark is Snowdon, the highest mountain in Wales.

items.prompt: Who first built the Tower of London?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Tower of London was first built by William the Conqueror after he became king in 1066.

items.prompt: What are the Yeoman Warders at the Tower of London also known as?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Tours are given by the Yeoman Warders, also known as Beefeaters. Visitors can also see the Crown Jewels there.

items.prompt: Which is England's largest national park?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Lake District is England's largest national park.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The National Trust is a government department.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The National Trust is a charity that works to preserve important buildings, coastline and countryside in the UK.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: National parks are areas of protected countryside that everyone can visit.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): National parks are areas of protected countryside that everyone can visit, and where people live, work and look after the landscape.

items.prompt: Which TWO are national parks?
distractors: The London Eye and the Lake District
The Eden Project and the London Eye
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): Snowdonia (North Wales) and the Lake District (England) are national parks.

items.prompt: Which TWO landmarks are in London?
items.answer: The London Eye and the Tower of London
distractors: The London Eye and the Giant's Causeway
Edinburgh Castle and the Tower of London
Edinburgh Castle and the Giant's Causeway
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The London Eye and the Tower of London are in London; Edinburgh Castle is in Scotland and the Giant's Causeway is in Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: Where is Skara Brae, the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Skara Brae on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland, is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.

items.prompt: In which English county does Stonehenge stand?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Stonehenge, a monument built during the Stone Age, still stands in the English county of Wiltshire.

items.prompt: Who were the first people to live in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The first people to live in Britain were hunter-gatherers, in what we call the Stone Age.

items.prompt: About how long ago did Britain become separated from the continent of Europe?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain was connected to the continent by a land bridge; it became permanently separated about 10,000 years ago.

items.prompt: Which famous Iron Age hill fort can still be seen in Dorset?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Iron Age people built hill forts; one of the most impressive, Maiden Castle, can still be seen in Dorset.

items.prompt: Which family of languages was spoken by people in Britain during the Iron Age?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): People in the Iron Age spoke languages belonging to the Celtic language family; related languages are still spoken in parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

items.prompt: Who led an unsuccessful Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Julius Caesar led a Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC; it was unsuccessful.

items.prompt: In which year did the Roman Emperor Claudius lead the invasion that began Roman rule in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): For nearly 100 years after 55 BC Britain was free of Romans; then Emperor Claudius led an invasion in AD 43.

items.prompt: Boudicca, who fought against the Romans, was queen of which tribe?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Boudicca, queen of the Iceni in what is now eastern England, fought against the Romans.

items.prompt: Why did Emperor Hadrian build a wall in the north of England?
distractors: To mark the border with Wales
To protect London from the Saxons
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parts of what is now Scotland were never conquered by the Romans, and Hadrian built a wall to keep out the Picts (ancestors of the Scottish people).

items.prompt: Which TWO places are popular sites to visit along Hadrian's Wall?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parts of Hadrian's Wall, including the forts of Housesteads and Vindolanda, can still be seen; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

items.prompt: In which year did the Roman army leave Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Roman army left Britain in AD 410 to defend other parts of the Roman Empire and never returned.

items.prompt: Which TWO things did the Romans bring to Britain?
distractors: The parliament and common law courts
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Romans built roads and public buildings, created a structure of law and introduced new plants and animals.

items.prompt: Which tribes invaded Britain after the Romans left?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the Romans left, Britain was invaded by tribes from northern Europe: the Jutes, the Angles and the Saxons.

items.prompt: What was found at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk?
items.answer: The burial ship of an Anglo-Saxon king
distractors: The remains of a Roman fort
A Viking longship and its crew
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): An Anglo-Saxon king was buried with treasure and armour in a ship at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk.

items.prompt: Who founded a monastery on the island of Iona, off the coast of Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Missionaries came to Britain to spread Christianity; St Columba founded a monastery on Iona.

items.prompt: Who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): St Augustine led missionaries from Rome who spread Christianity in the south; he became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

items.prompt: From which countries did the Vikings come?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway.

items.prompt: In which year did the Vikings first visit Britain to raid coastal towns?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Vikings first visited Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take away goods and slaves.

items.prompt: Which Anglo-Saxon king united the kingdoms and defeated the Vikings?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England united under King Alfred the Great, who defeated the Vikings.

items.prompt: Which TWO English place names come from the Viking languages?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many place names, such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe, come from the Viking languages.

items.prompt: Under which king did the people in the north unite, so that the word 'Scotland' came into use?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The threat of Viking attack encouraged people in the north to unite under one king, Kenneth MacAlpin, and the term Scotland began to be used.

items.prompt: Who won the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated Harold, the Saxon king of England, at the Battle of Hastings.

items.prompt: What does the Bayeux Tapestry show?
distractors: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Battle of Hastings is commemorated in a great piece of embroidery known as the Bayeux Tapestry, which can still be seen in France.

items.prompt: What was the Domesday Book?
items.answer: A record of towns, villages, land and animals
distractors: A list of laws agreed by King John
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William sent people all over England to draw up lists of towns and villages, who lived there, who owned the land and what animals they owned; this was the Domesday Book.

items.prompt: What is the Norman Conquest of 1066 remembered as?
items.answer: The last successful foreign invasion of England
distractors: The first Viking raid on England
The end of the Wars of the Roses
The start of the Hundred Years War
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Norman Conquest was the last successful foreign invasion of England and led to many changes in government and social structures.

items.prompt: Which king conquered Wales and built castles such as Conwy and Caernarvon?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1284 King Edward I of England introduced the Statute of Rhuddlan, which annexed Wales to the Crown; huge castles, including Conwy and Caernarvon, were built to maintain his power.

items.prompt: Who defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1314 the Scottish, led by Robert the Bruce, defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn, and Scotland remained unconquered.

items.prompt: When the English first went to Ireland in the Middle Ages, which area did they control?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the Middle Ages the English controlled an area of Ireland known as the Pale, around Dublin.

items.prompt: How long did the so-called Hundred Years War with France actually last?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English kings fought a long war with France called the Hundred Years War, even though it actually lasted 116 years.

items.prompt: Which king led the English to victory at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): One of the most famous battles of the Hundred Years War was the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, where King Henry V's vastly outnumbered English army defeated the French.

items.prompt: In which year did the Black Death come to Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1348 a disease, probably a form of plague, came to Britain; this was known as the Black Death.

items.prompt: What proportion of the population of England died in the Black Death?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): One third of the population of England died in the Black Death, and a similar proportion in Scotland and Wales.

items.prompt: In which year was the Magna Carta agreed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Magna Carta, meaning the Great Charter, was agreed in 1215.

items.prompt: What important idea did the Magna Carta establish?
items.answer: The king was subject to the law
distractors: Everyone had the right to vote
The Church was free from the Pope
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Magna Carta established the idea that even the king was subject to the law.

items.prompt: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a series of poems in English about people on a pilgrimage to Canterbury, called The Canterbury Tales.

items.prompt: Who was the first person in England to print books using a printing press?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William Caxton was the first person in England to print books using a printing press; The Canterbury Tales was one of the first books printed.

items.prompt: Which two houses fought each other in the Wars of the Roses?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1455 a civil war, the Wars of the Roses, began to decide who should be king of England, fought between the House of Lancaster and the House of York.

items.prompt: In which year did the Battle of Bosworth Field end the Wars of the Roses?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The war ended with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.

items.prompt: Which king was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): King Richard III of the House of York was killed in the Battle of Bosworth Field.

items.prompt: Which of Henry VIII's wives was a Spanish princess?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess; when she failed to give him a son, Henry wanted a divorce.

items.prompt: Which wife of Henry VIII was the mother of Elizabeth I?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Anne Boleyn was English and had one daughter, Elizabeth; she was executed at the Tower of London.

items.prompt: Which wife of Henry VIII gave birth to his son Edward?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry married Jane Seymour, who gave him the son he wanted, Edward; she died shortly after the birth.

items.prompt: Which wife of Henry VIII outlived him?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Catherine Parr was a widow who married Henry late in his life; she survived him and married again but died soon after.

items.prompt: Why did Henry VIII establish the Church of England?
items.answer: The Pope refused to let him divorce
distractors: He wanted to become a Catholic priest
Parliament ordered him to do so
The Spanish king asked him to
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): To divorce his first wife Henry needed the Pope's approval; when the Pope refused, Henry established the Church of England, in which the king had the power to appoint bishops.

items.prompt: Which Act formally united Wales with England during the reign of Henry VIII?
items.answer: The Act for the Government of Wales
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): During the reign of Henry VIII, Wales became formally united with England by the Act for the Government of Wales.

items.prompt: Which book was written during the reign of Edward VI and is still used in some Church of England services?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Edward VI was strongly Protestant; during his reign the Book of Common Prayer was written, a version of which is still used in some Church of England churches.

items.prompt: Which monarch, a devout Catholic, persecuted Protestants and became known as 'Bloody Mary'?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Edward VI was followed by his half-sister Mary, a devout Catholic who persecuted Protestants; she became known as 'Bloody Mary'.

items.prompt: In which year did England defeat the Spanish Armada?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth I became one of the most popular monarchs, particularly after the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588.

items.prompt: What was Sir Francis Drake's ship called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Sir Francis Drake, one of the commanders against the Armada, was one of the founders of England's naval tradition; his ship, the Golden Hind, was one of the first to sail around the world.

items.prompt: Where was William Shakespeare born?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, England, in 1564.

items.prompt: Which famous line comes from Shakespeare?
items.answer: To be or not to be
distractors: We shall fight on the beaches
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Lines from Shakespeare's plays are still quoted, such as 'To be or not to be' and 'Once more unto the breach'.

items.prompt: When Elizabeth I died in 1603, who became King of England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth I never married and had no children; when she died in 1603 her heir was her cousin James VI of Scotland, who also became James I of England, Wales and Ireland.

items.prompt: Which translation of the Bible was produced under James I?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): During James I's reign a new translation of the Bible into English, the 'King James Version' or 'Authorised Version', was made; it is still used in many Protestant churches today.

items.prompt: What were the 'plantations' in Ireland under James I?
items.answer: Settlements of Protestants on land in Ulster
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Under James I, many Protestant settlers from England and Scotland were given land in Ulster, taking it from Catholic landholders; these settlements were known as plantations.

items.prompt: What did James I and his son Charles I believe in?
distractors: A Catholic Church led by the Pope
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James I and his son Charles I believed in the 'Divine Right of Kings': the idea that the king was directly appointed by God to rule.

items.prompt: What were supporters of the king called in the English Civil War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Those who supported the king were called Cavaliers; those who supported Parliament were called Roundheads.

items.prompt: Which TWO battles did Parliament's army win against Charles I?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles I's army was defeated by Parliament at the Battles of Marston Moor and Naseby; by 1646 Parliament had won the war.

items.prompt: In which year was Charles I executed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles I was executed in 1649 after refusing to make an agreement with Parliament.

items.prompt: What title did Oliver Cromwell take as leader of the republic?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): With no king, England declared itself a republic called the Commonwealth; Oliver Cromwell was given the title of Lord Protector and ruled until his death in 1658.

items.prompt: In which year was the monarchy restored with Charles II?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In May 1660 Parliament invited Charles II to come back from exile in the Netherlands; this period is called the Restoration.

items.prompt: Which scientific society, the oldest surviving one in the world, was formed during the reign of Charles II?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Royal Society was formed to promote 'natural knowledge'; it is the oldest surviving scientific society in the world.

items.prompt: Who designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A great fire destroyed much of London in 1666, including many churches; St Paul's Cathedral was rebuilt to a design by Sir Christopher Wren.

items.prompt: What did the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 guarantee?
items.answer: That every prisoner has a right to a court hearing
distractors: That Parliament would meet every three years
That the monarch must be Protestant
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Habeas Corpus Act became law in 1679; it guaranteed that no one could be held prisoner unlawfully, as every prisoner has a right to a court hearing.

items.prompt: Who was invited to invade England in 1688 in what became known as the Glorious Revolution?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1688 important Protestants asked William of Orange, the Protestant ruler of the Netherlands and husband of James II's daughter Mary, to invade England.

items.prompt: Why is the revolution of 1688 called 'Glorious'?
items.answer: There was no fighting in England
distractors: It ended the Hundred Years War
It gave all men the right to vote
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William's invasion was called the Glorious Revolution because there was no fighting in England and because it guaranteed the power of Parliament.

items.prompt: Which document of 1689 confirmed the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Bill of Rights, 1689, confirmed the rights of Parliament and the limits of the king's power.

items.prompt: Who were the Huguenots who came to Britain between 1680 and 1720?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Between 1680 and 1720 many refugees called Huguenots came from France; they were Protestants who had been persecuted for their religion.

items.prompt: What was created by the Act of Union of 1707?
distractors: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Act of Union, known as the Treaty of Union in Scotland, was agreed in 1707, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain.

items.prompt: After Queen Anne died in 1714, who did Parliament choose as king?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Queen Anne had no surviving children; Parliament chose a German, George I, to be the next king, because he was Anne's nearest Protestant relative.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Henry VII strengthened the central administration of England and reduced the power of the nobles.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII wanted England to remain peaceful and his position to be secure, so he strengthened central administration and reduced the power of the nobles.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: When the Vikings first came to Britain, they came to settle peacefully as farmers.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Vikings first visited Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take away goods and slaves; later some stayed and settled.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The first farmers in Britain probably came from south-east Europe.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The first farmers arrived about 6,000 years ago, probably from south-east Europe.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Stonehenge is in Scotland.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Stonehenge stands in the English county of Wiltshire; Skara Brae is the prehistoric village on Orkney, Scotland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Romans conquered all of what is now Scotland.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parts of what is now Scotland were never conquered by the Romans; Hadrian built a wall to keep out the Picts.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Vikings who settled in England lived mainly in the south and west.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many Vikings stayed in the east and north of England, in an area known as the Danelaw.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Harold was the Saxon king of England who was killed at the Battle of Hastings.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold, the Saxon king of England, at the Battle of Hastings.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Normans conquered Scotland after the Battle of Hastings.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Normans did not conquer Scotland; the Battle of Hastings made William king of England.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Norman French and Anglo-Saxon gradually combined to form the English language.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the Norman Conquest, Norman French and Anglo-Saxon gradually blended to become one language, known as English.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Black Death led to a shortage of workers and the growth of new social classes.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the Black Death there were fewer people; labour shortages led to new social classes, including owners of large areas of land (later called the gentry).

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Magna Carta gave every adult the right to vote.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Magna Carta restricted the king's power and showed that even the king was subject to the law; only a small part of the population could vote for centuries afterwards.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the Middle Ages, judges in England developed 'common law' based on precedent and tradition.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Judges developed 'common law' through a process of precedence (following previous decisions) and tradition.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The House of Lancaster's symbol was a white rose.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The symbol of Lancaster was a red rose and the symbol of York was a white rose.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Tudor rose combines the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII's marriage united the families; the red and white Tudor rose became the symbol of the House of Tudor.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Catherine Howard was a cousin of Anne Boleyn and was executed.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Catherine Howard was a cousin of Anne Boleyn; she was accused of taking lovers and was executed.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Elizabeth I re-established the Church of England.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth I was a Protestant and re-established the Church of England as the official Church.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed on the orders of Elizabeth I.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth I held Mary prisoner for 20 years and later executed her, accusing her of plotting to overthrow her.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: James I of England had already been King of Scotland before 1603.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James VI of Scotland became James I of England, Wales and Ireland when Elizabeth I died in 1603.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The English Civil War began in 1688.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Civil War began in 1642, when Charles I tried to arrest five parliamentary leaders, and civil war began between the king and Parliament.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Great Fire of London happened in 1666.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A great fire destroyed much of London in 1666, including many churches.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: James II was a Protestant king.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James II was a Roman Catholic; his daughters Mary and Anne were Protestants.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: William III defeated James II at the Battle of the Boyne in Ireland in 1690.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James II tried to regain the throne with an army in Ireland; William defeated him at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, an event still celebrated by some in Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Act of Union of 1707, Scotland kept its own legal and education systems.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Under the Act of Union Scotland was no longer an independent country, but it kept its own legal and education systems and Presbyterian Church.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: From 1695, newspapers in Britain needed a government licence.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): From 1695 newspapers were allowed to operate without a government licence, and more and more were published.

items.prompt: Which TWO disasters struck London in 1665 and 1666?
items.answer: The Great Plague and the Great Fire
distractors: The Black Death and the Great Flood
The Armada and the Gunpowder Plot
The Civil War and the Restoration
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): London suffered the Great Plague in 1665 and a great fire in 1666 that destroyed much of the city.

items.prompt: Which TWO of Henry VIII's wives did he divorce?
items.answer: Catherine of Aragon and Anne of Cleves
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry divorced Catherine of Aragon when she did not give him a son, and divorced Anne of Cleves soon after their political marriage.

items.prompt: Which TWO of Henry VIII's wives were executed?
distractors: Catherine of Aragon and Jane Seymour
Anne of Cleves and Catherine Parr
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard were both executed; Catherine of Aragon and Anne of Cleves were divorced, Jane Seymour died after childbirth and Catherine Parr survived Henry.

items.prompt: Which TWO political groups developed in Parliament after the Glorious Revolution?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Two main groups developed in Parliament, the Whigs and the Tories; the modern Conservative Party is still sometimes referred to as the Tories.

items.prompt: Which TWO cathedrals are examples of the great buildings of the Middle Ages?
distractors: St Paul's Cathedral and Westminster Cathedral
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the Middle Ages great cathedrals such as Lincoln Cathedral and York Minster were built, many with stained glass windows.

items.prompt: Who is generally regarded as the first Prime Minister of Great Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Robert Walpole led the government from 1721 to 1742 and is regarded as the first Prime Minister.

items.prompt: In 1745 Charles Edward Stuart tried to take the throne. By what name is he popularly known?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles Edward Stuart, grandson of James II, became known as Bonnie Prince Charlie.

items.prompt: At which battle was Bonnie Prince Charlie defeated in 1746?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles Edward Stuart's army was defeated at the Battle of Culloden in 1746, after which he escaped back to Europe.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After his defeat at Culloden, Bonnie Prince Charlie was crowned King of Scotland.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Bonnie Prince Charlie was defeated at Culloden in 1746 and escaped back to Europe; he never became king.

items.prompt: What happened during the Highland Clearances?
items.answer: Landlords destroyed small farms to make space for sheep and cattle
distractors: Forests were cut down to build warships
Coal mines were closed across the Highlands
Castles were demolished on the king's orders
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the Highland Clearances many Scottish landlords destroyed individual small farms (crofts) to make space for large flocks of sheep and herds of cattle.

items.prompt: Which Scottish poet, known as 'The Bard', wrote 'Auld Lang Syne'?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Robert Burns (1759–96) wrote in Scots, English and a mixture of both; his best-known work includes 'Auld Lang Syne'.

items.prompt: During the Enlightenment, Adam Smith developed important ideas in which field?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Adam Smith, a figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, developed ideas about economics which are still referred to today.

items.prompt: Which Enlightenment thinker's ideas about human nature continue to influence philosophers?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): David Hume's ideas about human nature continue to influence philosophers.

items.prompt: James Watt's scientific work, which helped the Industrial Revolution, was about what?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James Watt's work on steam power helped the progress of the Industrial Revolution.

items.prompt: What did the Bessemer process make possible?
distractors: The mass production of cotton cloth
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Bessemer process for the mass production of steel led to the development of the shipbuilding and railway industries.

items.prompt: Why were canals built during the Industrial Revolution?
items.answer: To link factories to towns, cities and ports
distractors: To supply drinking water to London
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Canals were built to link the factories to towns and cities and to the ports, particularly in the new industrial areas of the middle and north of England.

items.prompt: Sake Dean Mahomet opened Britain's first curry house in London in 1810. What was it called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Sake Dean Mahomet opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in George Street, London, in 1810.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Sake Dean Mahomet introduced 'shampooing', a type of Indian head massage, to Britain.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Sake Dean Mahomet and his wife introduced shampooing to Britain and he was appointed 'Shampooing Surgeon' to Kings George IV and William IV.

items.prompt: Which group set up the first formal anti-slavery groups in Britain in the late 1700s?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The first formal anti-slavery groups were set up by the Quakers in the late 1700s.

items.prompt: Which evangelical Christian and MP played an important part in ending the slave trade?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William Wilberforce, an evangelical Christian and MP, played an important part in changing the law against slavery.

items.prompt: In which year did it become illegal to trade slaves in British ships or from British ports?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1807 it became illegal to trade slaves in British ships or from British ports.

items.prompt: In which year was slavery abolished throughout the British Empire by the Emancipation Act?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1833 the Emancipation Act abolished slavery throughout the British Empire.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After slavery was abolished, about 2 million Indian and Chinese workers were employed to replace the freed slaves.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After 1833, 2 million Indian and Chinese workers were employed to replace the freed slaves.

items.prompt: In which year did the 13 American colonies declare their independence?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The colonists declared independence in 1776; Britain recognised it in 1783.

items.prompt: In which battle of 1805 did Admiral Nelson defeat the combined French and Spanish fleets?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Nelson won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed in the battle.

items.prompt: Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815; he later became Prime Minister.

items.prompt: The Union Flag of 1801 combines the crosses of which three patron saints?
items.answer: St George, St Andrew and St Patrick
distractors: St George, St David and St Andrew
St David, St Patrick and St Andrew
St George, St David and St Patrick
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The 1801 Union Flag combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick, after the Act of Union with Ireland.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Welsh dragon appears on the Union Flag.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Union Flag does not include the Welsh dragon, because Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created.

items.prompt: How old was Victoria when she became queen in 1837?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Queen Victoria became queen in 1837 aged 18 and reigned until 1901, almost 64 years.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: By the end of the Victorian period the British Empire had fewer than 50 million people.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): By the end of the Victorian period the British Empire was the largest empire the world has ever seen, with an estimated population of more than 400 million people.

items.prompt: What was one effect of the Reform Act of 1832?
items.answer: It greatly increased the number of people with the right to vote
distractors: It gave women the right to vote
It abolished the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Reform Act of 1832 greatly increased the number of people with the right to vote and abolished most 'rotten' and 'pocket' boroughs.

items.prompt: In the 1830s and 1840s, which group campaigned for further reform of voting?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the 1830s and 1840s a group called the Chartists campaigned for reform.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Until 1870, a married woman kept full control of her own earnings and property.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Until 1870 a married woman's earnings, property and money automatically belonged to her husband; Acts of 1870 and 1882 gave wives the right to keep them.

items.prompt: Which campaigner, born in Manchester in 1858, set up the Women's Social and Political Union?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903; its members became known as suffragettes.

items.prompt: In 1918 women gained the right to vote at what minimum age?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1918 women over the age of 30 were given voting rights; in 1928 women got the vote at 21, the same as men.

items.prompt: Which TWO statements about women's voting rights are correct?
items.answer: Women over 30 could vote from 1918 and women over 21 from 1928
distractors: Women over 21 could vote from 1918 and women over 18 from 1928
Women over 30 could vote from 1928 and women over 21 from 1945
Women over 18 could vote from 1918 and women over 30 from 1928
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Women over 30 got the vote in 1918; in 1928 women received the vote at 21, the same age as men.

items.prompt: Florence Nightingale became famous for her work in which war?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1854 Florence Nightingale went to Turkey and treated soldiers fighting in the Crimean War.

items.prompt: Florence Nightingale founded the Nightingale Training School for nurses at which hospital?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1860 she established the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London. She is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.

items.prompt: Which TWO projects are associated with the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel?
items.answer: The Great Western Railway and the Clifton Suspension Bridge
distractors: The Forth Bridge and the Channel Tunnel
Tower Bridge and the Severn Bridge
The Great Western Railway and the Forth Bridge
