items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can complain by going to a police station or writing to the Chief Constable of the police force involved.

items.prompt: In England and Wales, where are most minor criminal cases dealt with?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In England, Wales and Northern Ireland most minor criminal cases are dealt with in a magistrates' court.

items.prompt: Who normally decides cases in a magistrates' court in England and Wales?
items.answer: Unpaid magistrates from the local community
distractors: A judge and a jury of 12
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Magistrates (Justices of the Peace) are usually unpaid volunteers and do not need legal qualifications.

items.prompt: In Scotland, where are minor criminal offences dealt with?
items.answer: A Justice of the Peace Court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In Scotland, minor criminal offences go to a Justice of the Peace Court.

items.prompt: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where are serious criminal cases tried?
items.answer: In the Crown Court, before a judge and jury
distractors: In a magistrates' court, before three magistrates
In a County Court, before a single judge
In a Youth Court, before a jury
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Serious offences are tried in front of a judge and a jury in a Crown Court.

items.prompt: How many people sit on a jury in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A jury in Scotland has 15 members; in England, Wales and Northern Ireland a jury has 12 members.

items.prompt: Who is usually tried in a Youth Court?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): If an accused person is aged 10 to 17, the case is normally heard in a Youth Court.

items.prompt: What is the small claims procedure?
items.answer: An informal way to settle minor disputes without needing a lawyer
distractors: A way to appeal against a prison sentence
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The small claims procedure helps people settle minor disputes without spending a lot of money on a lawyer.

items.prompt: Where can you get free, confidential advice on legal and other problems?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Citizens Advice can give free and confidential advice and can help you find a solicitor.

items.prompt: Which organisation collects taxes in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Income tax and National Insurance are collected by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC).

items.prompt: What do National Insurance contributions help to pay for?
items.answer: State benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Money raised from National Insurance contributions pays for state benefits and services such as the state pension and the NHS.

items.prompt: What is the minimum age for driving a car in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You must be at least 17 years old to drive a car and must have a driving licence.

items.prompt: When must a car have an MOT test?
items.answer: Every year once it is over three years old
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): If your vehicle is over three years old, you must take it for a Ministry of Transport (MOT) test every year.

items.prompt: What do school governors do?
items.answer: Help set the strategic direction of a school and check its performance
distractors: Teach lessons when teachers are ill
Inspect school buildings for the police
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): School governors set the strategic direction of the school, ensure accountability and monitor and evaluate school performance.

items.prompt: Where can MPs regularly meet people from their constituency?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Many MPs hold regular local 'surgeries' where constituents can go in person to talk about issues.

items.prompt: How can members of the public watch debates in the House of Commons?
items.answer: From the public galleries, free of charge
distractors: Only if they are invited by the monarch
Only by paying a large fee
They are never allowed to watch
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can watch debates from the public galleries in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords; entry is free.

items.prompt: Which numbers can you call in an emergency to reach the police, fire or ambulance services?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In an emergency, call 999 or 112 and ask for the police, fire service or ambulance.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The UK constitution is not written down in any single document.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The constitution is made up of laws, conventions and court judgments rather than one document.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Members of the House of Lords are elected by the public.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Members of the House of Lords (peers) are not elected; they are appointed or inherit their seats.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: MPs are elected using a system called 'first past the post'.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In each constituency the candidate with the most votes is elected.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Speaker supports the government party in debates.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Speaker is politically neutral and keeps order in debates.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: British citizens aged 18 or over who are registered can vote in general elections.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The voting age is 18, and you must be on the electoral register.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Only people who were born in the UK can vote in UK general elections.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): UK citizens, citizens of the Irish Republic and eligible Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK can vote.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Citizens of the Irish Republic who live in the UK can vote in all public elections.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Adult citizens of the UK, Commonwealth and Irish Republic who are resident in the UK can vote in all public elections.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: All civil servants are replaced when a new party forms the government.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Civil servants are politically neutral and continue in their jobs whichever party is in power.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The monarch can advise, warn and encourage the Prime Minister.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The monarch has regular meetings with the Prime Minister and can advise, warn and encourage, but decisions are made by the government.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A jury in Scotland has 12 members.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Juries in Scotland have 15 members; in England, Wales and Northern Ireland they have 12.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Courts can issue Forced Marriage Protection Orders to protect people at risk of a forced marriage.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Forced marriage is a serious abuse of human rights, and courts can make protection orders for people at risk.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Female genital mutilation (FGM) is illegal in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): FGM is a crime in the UK, as is taking a girl abroad for FGM.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A husband cannot be charged with raping his wife.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Any man who forces a woman to have sex, including her husband, can be charged with rape.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The UK is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UK is one of five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The European Convention on Human Rights was drawn up by the United Nations.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): It was drawn up by the Council of Europe, not the UN.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Cars over three years old must pass an MOT test every year.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Vehicles over three years old need a valid MOT certificate each year.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: You can drive a car on UK roads from the age of 16.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You must be at least 17 to drive a car.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Magistrates in England and Wales are usually unpaid and do not need legal qualifications.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Magistrates (JPs) are usually unpaid volunteers from the local community.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Police and Crime Commissioners are appointed by the Prime Minister.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Police and Crime Commissioners are elected by the public.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Many MPs hold local 'surgeries' where constituents can meet them.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Surgeries let constituents raise issues with their MP in person.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Members of the public are not allowed to watch debates in the House of Commons.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The public can watch debates free of charge from the public galleries.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: People who are self-employed usually need to complete a self-assessment tax return.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Self-employed people must pay their own tax through self-assessment.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: It is legal for an employer to refuse someone a job because of their religion.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): UK law prohibits discrimination at work on grounds including religion or belief, sex, race, disability, sexual orientation and age.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A by-election chooses a new MP for a single constituency.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A by-election is held when an MP dies or resigns.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Human Rights Act 1998 removed the European Convention on Human Rights from UK law.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the Convention into UK law.

items.prompt: Which TWO make up the two Houses of Parliament?
items.answer: The House of Commons and the House of Lords
distractors: The House of Commons and the Supreme Court
The Cabinet and the civil service
The House of Lords and the local council
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Parliament has two Houses: the elected House of Commons and the House of Lords.

items.prompt: Which TWO are rights protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?
items.answer: The right to life and freedom from torture
distractors: The right to a free house and the right to a car
The right to avoid tax and the right to refuse jury service
The right to carry a weapon and the right to a free car
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Convention protects rights such as the right to life, prohibition of torture, freedom from slavery, liberty and a fair trial.

items.prompt: Which TWO must you have to drive a car legally on UK roads?
items.answer: A valid driving licence and motor insurance
distractors: A passport and a TV licence
A bank account and a library card
A council tax bill and a passport
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You must have a valid driving licence, and it is a criminal offence to drive without insurance.

items.prompt: Which TWO services are usually provided by local councils?
distractors: National Insurance and the armed forces
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Local authorities provide services such as education, housing, rubbish collection and libraries.

items.prompt: Which TWO groups can vote in UK general elections if they are 18 and resident here?
items.answer: Irish citizens and eligible Commonwealth citizens
distractors: Tourists and visiting students from any country
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): UK citizens, citizens of the Irish Republic and eligible Commonwealth citizens resident in the UK can vote in general elections.

items.prompt: Which TWO are good ways to help protect the environment?
items.answer: Recycling waste and walking or cycling for short journeys
distractors: Leaving lights on and driving everywhere
Burning rubbish and throwing away glass
Using the car for short trips and wasting water
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Recycling, and walking, cycling or using public transport, help reduce pollution; buying local food also helps.

items.prompt: Which TWO statements about the Speaker are correct?
items.answer: They are politically neutral and are chosen by MPs in a secret ballot
distractors: They lead the government and appoint the Cabinet
They are appointed by the monarch and lead the opposition
They are elected by the public and chair the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Speaker is neutral, chosen by other MPs in a secret ballot, and keeps order in debates.

items.prompt: Which TWO can sit in the House of Lords?
items.answer: Life peers and senior bishops of the Church of England
distractors: Police and Crime Commissioners and councillors
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The House of Lords includes life peers, hereditary peers and senior bishops of the Church of England.

items.prompt: Which TWO international organisations is the UK a member of?
distractors: The African Union and the United Nations
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UK is a member of the United Nations, NATO, the Commonwealth and the Council of Europe.

items.prompt: What is the National Eisteddfod of Wales?
items.answer: An annual cultural festival, largely in Welsh
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The National Eisteddfod of Wales is an annual cultural festival which includes music, dancing, art and original performances, largely in Welsh.

items.prompt: Which culture does the Notting Hill Carnival in London celebrate?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): The Notting Hill Carnival takes place in Notting Hill, London, every August and is a celebration of Caribbean culture.

items.prompt: In which London street is the Cenotaph, where the national Remembrance service is held?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 4 (A modern, thriving society): On Remembrance Day, wreaths are laid at the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London.

items.prompt: Which work by Isaac Newton showed how gravity applied to the whole universe?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Isaac Newton's most famous published work was Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), which showed how gravity applied to the whole universe.
